nodes.obligation: State the definition of the essential supremum norm and prove that the L^p norms of an essentially bounded measurable function on [0,1] tend to its essential-supremum norm as the exponent tends to infinity.
reader_obligations: State the goal as a limit, not as two inequalities, and keep both halves of the problem (definition and limit) in view.

anchors.note: The Lean theorem proves the limit only; the requested definition is never stated there.

nodes.obligation: Define the norm as the essential supremum: the least M with |f| at most M almost everywhere.
reader_obligations: State the definition in the form that makes positive measure of each super-level set below the norm immediate.

anchors.note: The Lean proof does not state the definition. It uses Mathlib's eLpNorm at exponent top and rewrites it to an essential supremum only once, inside the positive-measure step. Difference from the informal proof, which states the infimum definition first.

nodes.obligation: On the probability space [0,1], the L^p norm is at most the essential-supremum norm for every exponent p at least 1.
reader_obligations: Say where unit measure of the space is used: it removes the measure factor in the comparison of L^p norms.

anchors.note: The informal proof computes the integral of |f|^p. Lean cites one comparison lemma in `upper_bound`, and the main theorem does not call that lemma: it uses monotonicity of the L^p norm in the exponent directly.

nodes.obligation: For every positive real t, the powers t^{1/n} tend to 1 as the natural number n tends to infinity.
reader_obligations: Recognize this as the analytic fact that lets a fixed positive measure disappear from the lower bound.

anchors.note: Lean proves the limit in the reals along natural-number exponents only, by continuity of a constant base at exponent zero. The informal proof uses it for a real exponent p without proof.

nodes.obligation: For a level alpha strictly below the norm, choose beta strictly between alpha and the norm, and show the super-level set where the function exceeds beta is measurable with positive, finite measure.
reader_obligations: Justify positive measure from the definition of the essential supremum, and keep the chosen level fixed while the exponent varies.

anchors.ref: Fix $\alpha < \|f\|_\infty$. The set $E_\alpha = \{x : |f(x)| > \alpha\}$ has $m(E_\alpha) > 0$ by definition of ess sup
anchors.note: The informal proof uses the set where |f| exceeds alpha itself. Lean inserts a beta strictly between alpha and the norm and uses the set where the function exceeds beta.

nodes.obligation: Using the limit of B3 and the level set of B4, find one natural number n for which alpha is at most beta times the measure of the level set to the power 1/n, and hence at most the L^n norm on that set.
reader_obligations: See the lower bound as a bound on one fixed set: the L^p norm is at least the level times the measure of the set to the power 1/p.

anchors.note: Lean bounds the L^n norm on the level set by a Mathlib lemma (le_eLpNorm_of_bddBelow) and finds a single n from the limit, instead of stating the bound for every p as the informal proof does. Several steps convert between the extended nonnegative reals and the reals; they have no informal counterpart.

nodes.obligation: Extend the bound from that one exponent n to every exponent p at least n by monotonicity of the L^p norm on a probability space: eventually the L^p norm is at least alpha, for every alpha below the norm.
reader_obligations: Explain why a bound at one exponent gives the same bound at all larger exponents, and why it suffices to prove the lower bound for every level strictly below the norm.

anchors.note: The informal proof has the bound for all p at once and so has no extension step.

nodes.obligation: Combine the upper bound and the eventual lower bound into the limit: the L^p norms tend to the essential-supremum norm as p tends to infinity.
reader_obligations: Say how the two one-sided bounds produce a limit, and restore the full exponent range.

anchors.note: The informal proof squeezes liminf and limsup. Lean proves the tendsto by its order characterization: eventually above every lower bound and eventually below every upper bound. Same content, different framing.

Both mined nodes read as the claim that the L^p norm is at least the essential-supremum norm for each p, which is false; the source lines state bounds on liminf. Retained as a negative anchoring example.

profiles.audience: A mathematician who knows measure theory and wants the two-sided estimate.
profiles.compression: State the definition, give the upper bound in one line, and spend the space on the level-set choice and the lower bound; cite the power limit and the monotonicity extension without proof.

profiles.audience: A student who has not seen why the norm is approached from below by level sets.
profiles.compression: Show every node; spend the most exposition on why a level strictly below the norm has positive measure, and on why the bound at one exponent persists.

profiles.audience: A reviewer comparing the prose with the compiled Lean proof.
profiles.compression: Do not compress side conditions; expose the measurable representative equal almost everywhere, the intermediate level, the finite-measure check, and the monotonicity step that the informal proof lacks.
